name: Ivan Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no connection to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you're free to give me the public answer and the private one. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the live-line team at the Highwater depot, up in the valleys. Live-line means we work on the wires while they're still switched on, using long insulated poles we call hot sticks, so the farms and villages don't lose power while we fix things. Some days I drive two hours up a single-track road to change one insulator on a ridge.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the problem-solving, and the views, honestly. I talk to the AI on my phone in the truck most days, getting it to dig out the old line drawings or work out the best order for jobs. What grinds me down is that valley pay is lower than in town and Nadia's salon still has a loan on it, so we've got almost nothing put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. I'd be surprised, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's still a handy tool, it saves me half an hour a day hunting for drawings. With friends I'd say the hype guys got it wrong but the useful bits are real. Online I'd post something mildly smug about how I was using it right all along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my life stays as it is, which is fine but tight. I'd have liked the robot arms I've seen on videos from abroad to come here, because that would make live-line work safer. Without that, it's same job, same pay, same loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep using the tools I use now. I'd look at the robot arm trials happening elsewhere and ask the depot manager if we could be a test site. And I'd help Nadia set up an AI booking system for the salon, which might bring in a few more clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a tiny bit bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI in the truck every day. What's a typical thing you ask it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday I took a photo of a rusted plate on a pole and asked what year that type of transformer was made. It told me, and that told me what spares to bring up the hill. That's two hours saved, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the salon loan weigh on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three hundred a month for another two years. Nadia's busy before Christmas and dead in January, so January's when we feel it. We had to borrow from her dad last year for the car tax.

S0.say: He'd say AI is still a handy tool that saves him half an hour a day hunting drawings. Online he'd post something mildly smug about having used it right all along.
S0.think: Privately life stays fine but tight, and he'd miss the robot arms from foreign videos that would make live-line work safer. Same job, same pay, same loan.
S0.do: Keeps using his current AI tools and asks the depot manager to bid as a robot arm test site. Helps his partner set up an AI booking system for her salon.
S0.quote: I took a photo of a rusted plate on a pole and asked what year that type of transformer was made.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan uses AI in practical, specific ways and would be the one asking for trials. Money is tight because of his partner's salon loan, which hits hardest in January. He sees robots mainly as a safety gain for live-line work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we're talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that this is our chance to get the dangerous stuff off our hands and onto machines. With friends I'd say the ones who learn it early will do fine. I'd probably share videos of the robot arms in the crew chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I come out of this well. I already use the tools and I want the robot arm job. The thing that worries me is whether the company pays for skill or just squeezes more work out of fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the first robot arm trial at Highwater and do the operator certification as soon as it's offered. I'd learn whatever fault-prediction software comes in. If the company wouldn't pay for the course, I'd pay for it in instalments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Like the start of a new season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said those who learn early do fine. What about those who don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard part. Tom on my team has thirty years of hot-stick work and he hates screens. I'd want the company to keep him on as the expert who says whether the robot's doing it right, because he'd spot a mistake before any of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Paying in instalments with almost no savings. Is that wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, by the book. But if it gets me on the robot side, it pays back in a year. I've always been the one who jumps first and figures out the money after. Nadia rolls her eyes at that.

S1.say: He'd say this is the chance to get dangerous work off workers' hands and onto machines, and that early learners will do fine. He'd share robot arm videos in the crew chat.
S1.think: He thinks he comes out well because he already uses the tools and wants the robot arm job. His worry is whether the company pays for skill or just squeezes more from fewer people.
S1.do: Volunteers for the first robot arm trial at Highwater and takes the operator certification as soon as offered, paying in instalments if needed. Learns any new fault-prediction software.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like the start of a new season.
S1.quote: I've always been the one who jumps first and figures out the money after. Nadia rolls her eyes at that.
S1.fieldNote: He frames automation as a safety gain and a career step. He'd take a financial risk on training despite having no savings, and knows it. He wants experienced colleagues kept on as the people who check the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Two years is fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that we need to be smart about this, not scared, and that the people who know the network should be running the rollout. I'd say it to the manager, to my mates, everywhere. I wouldn't be one for protest signs, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd get maybe a year or two out of being the robot guy. After that, if the robots are cheaper and better at everything, my head start runs out. And Nadia's salon has a loan on it, so we'd be hit twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to whoever's installing robots on our network and ask to work for them, even if it means weeks away from home. I'd cut the extras right away, sell my motorbike, and put every spare bit towards paying off the salon loan early. Then I'd figure out the rest as it came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More awake than scared, if that makes sense. The mountains help, they'd be the last place the robots get to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the mountains be the last place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's hard ground. Steep slopes, snow, one road in. A robot on a flat estate is easy; a robot on a ridge in February is a different story. So I reckon Highwater buys me a bit of extra time compared to the town crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Weeks away from home with two young kids. What would Nadia say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say do what you need to do, then she'd be furious for a week. Rosie's seven, she'd miss me. But if it's that or losing the house, she'd rather I was away.

S2.say: He'd say people need to be smart, not scared, and that those who know the network should run the rollout. He wouldn't wave protest signs; that's not him.
S2.think: Privately he'd get a year or two out of being the robot guy before his head start runs out. His partner's salon loan means the household would be hit twice.
S2.do: Applies straight to whoever installs robots on his network, accepting weeks away from home. Sells his motorbike, cuts extras and puts every spare bit towards paying off the salon loan early.
S2.feel: Anxious but more awake than scared, taking some comfort that mountains would be the last place robots reach.
S2.quote: A robot on a flat estate is easy; a robot on a ridge in February is a different story.
S2.fieldNote: He believes his rough terrain buys him time, which steadies him. His plan is to chase the last human jobs in the rollout, even working away. He doesn't pretend his adaptability saves him long term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I like that better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is enough time for everyone to get ready, so let's not waste it. At work I'd tell the younger lads to get every certificate going. I'd post about the training courses and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to really build something. I'd get operator, then robot maintenance, then maybe supervising a fleet of them across the valleys. It's not forever, but it's a real run of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the robot operator course and start the maintenance qualification. I'd pay the salon loan off by year two and then start saving properly. I'd push the depot to trial robots early so I'm on the inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly because of money. The work side I'm actually looking forward to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a real run of work. What happens at the end of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. By then I'd be nearly fifty and hopefully the loan's gone and we've got a bit put by. I'd rather face that with five good years behind me than two scared ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you take with you onto the robot side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom, if he'd come. I'd do the screens, he'd do the judgment. A machine might know the rules, but Tom knows which pole was put in crooked in 1994.

S3.say: He'd say there's enough time for everyone to get ready, so don't waste it, and tell younger colleagues to get every certificate going. He'd post about training courses.
S3.think: He thinks five years is enough to build a real run of work, from operator to maintenance to supervising a robot fleet across the valleys.
S3.do: Takes the robot operator course and starts the maintenance qualification in year one. Pays off the salon loan by year two, then saves properly, and pushes the depot to trial robots early.
S3.feel: Uneasy mostly about money, but looking forward to the work side.
S3.quote: A machine might know the rules, but Tom knows which pole was put in crooked in 1994.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives him a staged career plan built around robots. He values his older colleague's knowledge and would team up with him. His unease is about the end point and money, not the change itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's loads of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to get caught out with a decade's notice. I'd tell the lads to treat it like an apprenticeship for the next job. I'd probably be the annoying one going on about it in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years doesn't scare me much. I'd have time to do the robot work and set up something on the side. The kids would be teenagers and grown, and the loan would be long gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robot certificates over the first few years. Around year three I'd start a small side business fixing drones and farm robots up the valleys, weekends at first. I'd talk to Leo about getting into robotics or something with his hands, and save what I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'd be more curious than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A side business with almost no savings. How would you start it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small. A van I've already got, a few tools, word of mouth from the farmers I already know. If it works, it grows. If it doesn't, I've lost a few weekends and a bit of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this decade that does scare you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the town people forget the valleys. Every new thing goes to the city first and reaches us last. I'd want to make sure the valley people are trained up too, not just left behind.

S4.say: He'd say there's no excuse for being caught out with a decade's notice and tell colleagues to treat it like an apprenticeship for the next job. He'd be the one going on about it in the canteen.
S4.think: Privately ten years doesn't scare him much: time for robot work plus a side business, with the kids grown and the loan long gone.
S4.do: Takes robot certificates over the first few years and around year three starts a weekend side business fixing drones and farm robots in the valleys. Talks with his son about robotics or hands-on work and saves what he can.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, more curious than worried.
S4.quote: Every new thing goes to the city first and reaches us last.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he becomes almost optimistic, planning a small business from his existing farm contacts. His only real fear is the valleys being left out. He accepts risk cheerfully, even with thin savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to turn being early into anything that lasts, and we'd be hit twice with the salon. What would help is paid training on the robots now, help paying off small business loans like Nadia's, and making sure the valley crews get the same chances as the town.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about safety. Live-line work kills people every year somewhere. If robots take that off us, that's something good, and I don't want it lost in all the worry.

headlineQuote: If robots take that off us, that's something good, and I don't want it lost in all the worry.
portrait: Ivan Walsh is a 43-year-old live-line worker in a remote valley depot, married to a salon owner with a business loan, with two kids and almost nothing saved. He uses AI every day in his truck and wants to operate the robot arms he's seen in foreign videos. He is calm in the plateau and steady pictures and sees automation as a safety gain. The two-year AGI picture makes him anxious, though he thinks the mountains buy him time, while five years means a staged robot career and ten years a side business fixing farm robots. His main fear beyond money is the valleys being left behind.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to turn being early into something lasting and the household would be hit twice through the salon loan.
whatWouldHelp: Paid robot training now, help paying off small business loans, and equal chances for valley crews and town crews.
